title: Let the target interface pick the overload

blocks.text: When a referenced method is overloaded, the compiler picks the overload by the **target type**: the parameter types of the functional interface stand in for the argument types of an ordinary call.

`List<Integer>` has two `remove` methods: `remove(int index)` and `remove(Object o)`. `String` has many `valueOf` methods, among them `valueOf(char[])` and `valueOf(Object)`. Write three factories in `Overloads`, each returning a method reference:

items: `ObjIntConsumer<List<Integer>> removeAt()` removes the element at the given **index**.
`Function<char[], String> text()` turns a character array into the string it spells.

blocks.text: The same method name can mean different things here; which one runs depends on the interface you return it as.

cases.says: removeAt removes by position, and removeValue works where value and position name the same element.
With an Integer argument, List::remove resolves to remove(Object) and removes that value, not the element at that index.
With a char[] argument, String::valueOf resolves to valueOf(char[]) and gives the characters as text.
removeValue finds the value with equals, so an Integer equal to one in the list removes it even when it is another object.

concepts: An overloaded method's reference resolves to the overload that the target interface's parameter types select.
